label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
Kelechi,

You said put it in writing. So here it is, in writing, on paper, in an envelope, with a stamp I queued for at the post office on Rye Lane like it's 1998. Read it on the train. If the man next to you is looking over your shoulder, tell him to mind his business, this one is private.

First of all, I was serious at my birthday. I know I'd had two Guinness and I was dancing like my knees are still 21, but I meant it. You should come and teach maths.

Before you start laughing, hear me out. I'm not going to preach. I know you hate that, and I know the moment I start sounding like a pastor you'll fold this paper and use it as a coaster. So I'll just tell you what I see, and what I know, and you decide.

**What I see**

Nine years, Kelechi. Nine years at that Croydon firm. Every time I see you, you tell me the same thing: same spreadsheet, same meeting, same man from the client side who doesn't read the email and then asks you what's in the email. I've heard that story so many times I could deliver it at your wedding. You're a very clever guy spending your days checking other people's costings. I'm not saying the job is nothing. Somebody has to make sure the building doesn't cost double. I'm just saying it doesn't have to be you forever.

And don't tell me you're "not a teacher." Have you forgotten Moremi? Before every exam half that hostel was in your room, sitting on your bed, on the floor, on top of your bucket, because you were the only person who could explain further maths without making anyone feel like a goat. You got an A in further maths and then you spent your own revision time dragging the rest of us through it. Nobody paid you. You just did it, because you're like that. I passed that course partly because of you, and I'm only admitting it now because you can't see my face.

Then Christmas. My nephew still talks about the jollof rice. You put rice on plates and showed him a half and a quarter and an eighth, and he understood fractions in maybe twenty minutes after his teacher had been trying since October. He's nine. He told my sister "Uncle Kelechi's maths is the food maths." That's what good teaching looks like. You explained it in a way that made sense to him and he never once felt stupid. Most people can't do that. You do it without even thinking.

**What I know**

At my school (Peckham, 1,100 kids) two of our Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher since September. They're nice people, but they come and go, and the kids know it. Those children are thirteen and fourteen and they're already deciding they're "not maths people," because nobody has stayed long enough to show them otherwise. That's the kind of gap someone like you could fill. I'm not saying you'd be in my school or in those exact classes, but there are classes like that everywhere in London, waiting for somebody who actually wants to be there.

Let me tell you about Damola. Year 11, good boy, plenty of mouth. For three weeks he could not get simultaneous equations. Three weeks. He was frustrated, I was frustrated, I tried everything. Then last month, one random Tuesday, he got it. He looked at the board, looked at his book, and shouted "IS THAT ALL??" and the whole class started clapping. Clapping, Kelechi. Thirty teenagers clapping for maths. I went to the staffroom afterwards and just sat there smiling like a fool. You don't get that from a spreadsheet. I promise you.

On your last birthday you said, "I just want to do something that matters before 40." I remember because you said it quietly, after the jokes had finished. You're 34. You have time. I'm not throwing your words back at you to win an argument, but you said them, and I believed you.

**The bad parts (because you won't believe the good parts otherwise)**

I'm not going to lie to you. Teaching is hard. The marking never ends. You finish one pile and another one is already there. Some days the behaviour is pure wahala. A kid will tell you something about your shoes or your head that you'll think about for the rest of the week. There'll be lessons you plan beautifully that go completely wrong because it's windy outside and everybody has lost their mind.

When I started in 2019 I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice. Full tears, in my car, engine off, before driving home. I'm not hiding that from you. The first year is hard and anybody who tells you otherwise is selling something.

But it gets better. It really does. You get your routines, you learn the kids, they learn you, and one day you realise you haven't cried in the car park in years and you actually look forward to period 3 with your Year 10s. I'm in my seventh year now and I'm still here because I want to be, not because I'm stuck.

Money. Yes, your pay will drop in the first year. I won't pretend it won't. But the route I'm talking about is the salaried one, so you get paid while you train. You won't be a broke student again eating indomie three times a day. It's one year, starting September 2027. After that the pay goes up, the pension is a proper pension, and the holidays... my guy, the holidays. I know you're going to say "but you work in the holidays." Some of it, yes. But I also went to Lagos for three weeks in August and nobody emailed me about a cost plan.

And before you say you're too old: a woman in my department started at 41. Forty-one. She's one of the best teachers we have, and the kids respect her because she's lived a bit and doesn't panic. Coming in from another job is an advantage. You've managed clients, deadlines, difficult people. A Year 9 class on a Friday afternoon is just difficult people who are shorter.

**What I'm actually asking**

I'm not asking you to quit tomorrow. I'm not asking you to sign anything, fill any form, or tell your manager anything. Calm down.

I'm asking you to come to one open evening.

**Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham.**

That's it. Go, listen, ask your annoying detailed questions (you know you will, you're a QS, you'll want the breakdown of everything), and then go home and think about it. If you go and it's not for you, fine. I'll never mention it again. Okay, I'll mention it maybe once a year, at my birthday, after two Guinness. But I won't push.

I'll come with you. I'll meet you there, or we can go together from London Bridge, whatever works. Afterwards I'll buy you food and you can tell me all the reasons it's a bad idea, and I'll listen.

Applications for next September open soon, so this is the right time to at least look. If you leave it, it becomes "maybe next year," and then you're 37 telling me about the same spreadsheet. I don't want that for you. I don't think you want it either.

You're patient, you're funny, and you explain things without making people feel small. Kids would love you. I'm not just saying that to flatter you. I've watched you do it since we were 18.

So. 19 November. 6pm. Lewisham. Text me when you've finished reading this, even if it's just to say I'm mad.

And yes, I know you're laughing that I posted a letter. Keep it. When you're Head of Maths somewhere, I'll want it framed.

Your guy,

---

*P.S. If you show this to anyone at your office, I'll deny everything.*
